I re-drove it at code head e2dcb986ec2438f5b483f5cd6cfabb47ed572951, on a Postgres 17 of my own on the issue volume, and went past the implementer's own commands: rather than reading the new Go test, I flooded the real compiled broker over one pipelined connection and read the three refusal shapes off the wire. Each is what the finding asked for. Beside that, the Go packages this round touched are ok (api, approval, config, brokertest, oidc, cmd/broker, cmd/dev-oidc-issuer, cmd/agent-secrets-devrelay), cmd/agent-secrets fails the same 13 tests as main name for name, and Dispatch's browser suite is 53 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.

proof.criterion: The review's Important finding, and the spec's Design: every answer of a page route carries Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Cache-Control: no-store and nosniff — a refusal past the shared per-address bucket included — and a browser is never told about a ServiceAccount token it did not send
proof.surface: the real compiled broker binary (packages/envoy/cmd/broker, built from this head) on 127.0.0.1:17777 over a real Postgres 17 and a real cmd/dev-oidc-issuer, flooded over one pipelined HTTP/1.1 connection, with the three other route shapes asked on that same spent bucket in the same connection
proof.command: 400 pipelined `GET /approve/<record>` on one socket, then, on the same socket and the same spent bucket, `GET /signin/status`, `GET /approve/assets/approve.css` and `POST /v1/credential-requests/<record>/approve` carrying a forged bearer token; each response's status line, headers and body read off the wire
proof.observed: 403 responses for 403 requests. The page route: 217 answered 302 to the sign-in inside the burst, then 183 answered `429 Too Many Requests` whose headers are `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'`, `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, `Referrer-Policy: same-origin`, `Retry-After: 1`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and whose body is the page's own HTML reading 'Too many requests have come from this address. Try again in a moment.' — it names neither a ServiceAccount nor a token. On the same spent bucket: GET /signin/status answered `429` JSON `{"code":"RATE_LIMITED","error":"too many requests from this address; try again later"}`, naming the address and no token; the stylesheet answered `200` with the CSS, so it spends nothing; and the account decide route with a forged bearer answered `429` JSON `{"code":"RATE_LIMITED","error":"too many requests with a ServiceAccount token; try again later"}`, the one shape that still names the token, for the caller that really sends one. Three shapes, one bucket, read in one connection.
proof.negativeControl: Two controls, both measured in the same run. The forged ServiceAccount token was refused before any verification and decided nothing: the record was still pending after the flood. And the flood costs a person nothing lasting — six seconds later, once the bucket had refilled, a fresh sign-in through the whole authorization-code flow read the record's page, one Approve answered 303, the request reads granted with one grant, and GET /signin/status carries that approval's own time.

observationsForTheReviewer: The config refactor reads the four sign-in settings by index into the exported mutable `SignInSettings` against a four-element `into` slice declared beside it (packages/envoy/internal/broker/config/config.go:932-942), which is the index coupling round 1's review listed as a minor finding; a fifth entry added to the exported slice without a fifth destination panics at boot. Nothing outside the module touches that var today and the boot test covers the four, so this is a note rather than a finding.

The new api/account_limit_test.go drives GET /approve/{record}, GET /signin/callback and GET /signin/status past the bucket, not POST /approve or POST /signin/logout. Both posts take the same authSignIn path, so the shape is the same; I did not drive them past the limit either.

Still true from earlier rounds, and still not a failure: a signed-in person of the domain who is not the approver is served the whole record page, with no decision form. The spec's design describes that page and A2 requires only that she decide nothing, which she does not.

The operator's note from round 3 stands and is this deployment's rather than this pull request's: the page's routes share one per-address bucket with Dispatch's ServiceAccount traffic, so with a load balancer in front and BROKER_TRUSTED_PROXY_HEADER unset every browser and Dispatch would key on one address. At 50/s with a burst of 200 per process, ordinary use is nowhere near it — my flood needed 400 pipelined requests on one socket to reach it at all.
